title: Beyond “Done”: Building Verification Loops for AI Agents
subtitle: A plain-language glossary for observing, fixing, and proving an agent’s work

sections.name: AI basics
sections.intro: The small set of AI terms every workshop builds on.

terms.definition: Software that performs tasks associated with human intelligence, such as understanding language, finding patterns, making predictions, or choosing actions.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the broad category. Models, language models, and agents are specific kinds of AI systems.
terms.hear: We use AI to summarize the feedback.

terms.definition: A trained mathematical system that turns input into a prediction or output.
terms.whyItMatters: The model is the engine that produces an answer. The surrounding product decides what context and tools it receives.
terms.hear: Which model is this using?

terms.definition: A model trained on large amounts of text to predict and produce language one token at a time.
terms.whyItMatters: LLMs power chat assistants and many agents, but they still generate predictions rather than retrieving guaranteed facts.
terms.hear: Send that prompt to the LLM.

terms.definition: A small unit of text that a language model reads or writes. A token may be a word, part of a word, or punctuation.
terms.whyItMatters: Context limits, speed, and API prices are measured in tokens.
terms.hear: That document uses too many tokens.

terms.definition: The instruction or input given to a model.
terms.whyItMatters: A clear prompt states the desired outcome, useful context, constraints, and how to recognize a good result.
terms.hear: Try the task again with a clearer prompt.

terms.definition: The finite amount of instructions, conversation, source material, and tool results a model can consider at one time.
terms.whyItMatters: Important information can be omitted or pushed out when the context becomes crowded.
terms.hear: That conversation filled the context window.

terms.definition: A fluent answer that contains invented or unsupported information.
terms.whyItMatters: Confident wording is not evidence. Important claims still need a source or another check.
terms.hear: Verify that citation in case the model hallucinated it.

terms.definition: Giving a model trusted source material and asking it to base its answer on that evidence.
terms.whyItMatters: Grounding makes answers easier to verify and reduces unsupported claims.
terms.hear: Ground the answer in the workshop materials.

terms.definition: A model operating in a loop with instructions and tools so it can take multiple steps toward a goal.
terms.whyItMatters: An agent can inspect results and continue working instead of stopping after one response.
terms.hear: Give the agent the goal and let it run the checks.

terms.definition: An agent calling an external capability such as reading a file, searching the web, running code, or sending a request.
terms.whyItMatters: Tools let a model affect systems and gather current evidence, which also means permissions and limits matter.
terms.hear: The agent needs a tool for that action.

sections.name: Why “done” isn’t evidence
sections.intro: Start here. These terms explain why an agent saying “done” is different from the work being done, and what you would need to see instead.

terms.definition: An agent’s own claim that a task is finished, with no evidence attached. In the workshop’s staged worker report, the waitlist form renders, submits, and shows a success message, and the report says “Done.” Nothing in the report checks whether the signup was saved.
terms.whyItMatters: You learn to treat “done” as a claim to check, not a result. The workshop’s habit is to ask for the receipt before accepting the work.
terms.hear: “Done” is a claim. Ask for the receipt.

terms.definition: A check that passes without testing what the feature is supposed to do. Watching the waitlist form submit and show a success message is a shallow check. When you reload the page, the signup is gone. A submit check does not show that anything persisted.
terms.whyItMatters: Helps you spot the green signal that people and agents trust in your own system, and ask what that signal actually proves.
terms.hear: So it was briefly done.

terms.definition: Specific, checkable statements that define “done” for a feature. The Midnight Snack Lab waitlist has three. First, a visitor who joins sees the same email and status after a reload. Second, the confirmation says waitlist only, with no guaranteed seat. Third, it promises an email only if a place opens.
terms.whyItMatters: If you write these down before any fix, you and your agent have something concrete to prove. You no longer have to argue about whether the feature looks done.
terms.hear: What done means

terms.definition: A lasting change an action causes beyond what the screen shows, such as a record written to storage. In the waitlist, joining should save the signup so it survives a reload. The success message on its own is not the side effect.
terms.whyItMatters: The proof bar says to check side effects. When you check what was stored instead of what was displayed, you catch a feature that only looks finished.
terms.hear: Check side effects.

terms.definition: A small key-value store built into the browser. A web page can save data there, and the data survives a reload. The waitlist prototype is supposed to save each signup in localStorage. The bug shows up when snack storage returns an empty localStorage after Ada joins.
terms.whyItMatters: Reading localStorage tells you whether a signup was actually saved. The page’s success message cannot tell you that.
terms.hear: "localStorage": {}

terms.definition: The cycle the workshop builds so that an agent’s work is accepted on evidence. It has four steps: build the check, give the agent a way to run it, keep the evidence, and decide when to stop. In practice, the agent observes the problem, fixes it, and proves the fix. It repeats until the check passes on the current code.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the main pattern you take home. When an agent can run a check itself, it gets a specific failure, makes a targeted fix, and has a clear point at which to stop.
terms.hear: Observe. Fix. Prove.

sections.name: Giving the agent eyes
sections.intro: An agent has only your code and a terminal. These terms cover the tools that let it check a browser app the way you would, and why a command works better than written instructions.

terms.definition: A file of written guidance that an agent reads before it starts work. The usual first attempt at verification is a paragraph in this file, such as “Always verify UI changes in a browser. Remember to reload.” The workshop treats this as the weaker option. The agent re-reads and re-interprets the paragraph on every run, and the paragraph leaves no evidence behind.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains why written instructions alone don’t make an agent verify consistently, and why the workshop turns those steps into a command.
terms.hear: Don’t write a paragraph. Build a lever.

terms.definition: A small command-line tool (CLI) that drives one specific app and reports what happened as structured output. The idea comes from Lauren Tan’s “Build the Lever” principle in pstack. In this workshop the lever is pnpm snack prove. It runs the same steps every time, uses fewer tokens than a throwaway script, can be tested, and leaves a receipt.
terms.whyItMatters: Gives your agent a reliable way to check its own work. It runs one command and reads the result instead of improvising its own checks.
terms.hear: Build a lever.

terms.definition: The workshop’s lever: a single file, lab/snack.ts, that works as a remote control for the waitlist app. Its commands fall into four groups. Health has up, doctor, and down. Drive has join, reload, and reset. Look has snapshot, storage, console, network, screenshot, and eval. Prove has prove and judge. snack drives a real Chrome window over the Chrome DevTools Protocol.
terms.whyItMatters: snack can make any check you would make by hand in DevTools, but from a terminal. That means your agent can see what you would see.
terms.hear: Your agent’s eyes, in your terminal.

terms.definition:
The rules that make snack easy for an agent to use:
- Results go out as JSON, so the agent reads fields instead of prose.
- Every error includes a next line that says what to run instead.
- help works on every command.
- doctor runs first.
- Anything destructive supports --dry-run, which shows what the command would do without doing it.
terms.whyItMatters: Follow these rules when you build a verifier for your own app. An agent can then act on the tool’s output without guessing.
terms.hear: Errors say what to do next.

terms.definition: The connection that Chrome’s DevTools uses to inspect and control a page. Because snack speaks CDP, it can read localStorage, console messages, and network activity, and it can take screenshots. It does all of this from a terminal instead of from the DevTools panels.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains how an agent that only has a terminal can make the same checks a person makes in DevTools: reloading the page, inspecting storage, and looking for errors.
terms.hear: Speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol.

terms.definition: snack doctor is a single read-only health check that you run before anything else. It confirms four things: the tools are installed, the app is running, the page shows the current code, and the last proof is still fresh. Every failing check says what to run next.
terms.whyItMatters: Evidence gathered against the wrong build counts as no evidence. Running doctor first keeps you from debugging the app when the setup is what’s broken.
terms.hear: Doctor first.

terms.definition: A browser-automation library. The proof uses it to act like a user: it fills in the Email field, clicks Join waitlist, and reloads the page. Playwright’s locators, such as page.getByLabel("Email"), wait for the page on their own, so the proof doesn’t need sleeps. You don’t need any prior Playwright experience.
terms.whyItMatters: Lets you write a proof that follows the real user path and doesn’t fail at random because of timing.
terms.hear: No sleeps.

sections.name: Defining done in a proof
sections.intro: These terms come from the workshop’s one coding exercise, which turns “done” into a function. The function should pass a correct app and fail the broken ones.

terms.definition: The one function in lab/exercises/prove.ts that defines “done” for the waitlist. It takes a fresh visitor through the form, reloads the page the way a user would, and records what survived: the status, the saved email, the confirmation, and storage. It must pass the correct app and fail each broken app that it is responsible for catching.
terms.whyItMatters: Writing this function is the workshop’s one coding exercise. Once it exists, your agent runs it with pnpm snack prove and gets a verdict instead of guessing.
terms.hear: Make prove refuse “looks done.”

terms.definition:
Four rules a proof must meet:
- Use the user’s path, never an internal shortcut.
- Check side effects, such as what is in storage and what survives the reload.
- Capture the trigger and the end state in one run and one receipt.
- Run doctor first, because evidence for the wrong build is no evidence.
terms.whyItMatters: Use these rules to judge any check, whether you wrote it or an agent did. A screenshot of success that breaks these rules isn’t proof.
terms.hear: A screenshot of success isn’t proof.

terms.definition: The steps a real user takes to use a feature. For the waitlist, the user types an email, clicks the button, and then reloads. A proof must follow this path. It should not call internal code or write to storage directly.
terms.whyItMatters: A test that follows the user path catches the bugs a user would hit. A shortcut can pass while the real flow is broken.
terms.hear: Never an internal shortcut.

terms.definition: The helper a proof uses to record one fact. It takes a name, the actual value, the expected value, and an optional hint. check() never throws an error, so a missing record is written down as a failed check. Playwright’s expect() does throw, and a proof that throws is reported as “can’t tell” rather than “broken.” The hint becomes the next line in the receipt.
terms.whyItMatters: If you use check() where you should, the proof says what’s wrong. If you use expect() after the reload, the proof just crashes.
terms.hear: check() never throws.

terms.definition: A check with a fixed right answer that a program can compare exactly, such as “status after reload equals waitlisted.” The workshop’s advice is to start with assertions. Add a judgment from a model or a human only when a claim is about meaning.
terms.whyItMatters: Assertions are cheap, repeatable, and unambiguous, so most of your proof should be made of them. Knowing what they can’t check tells you when you need a meaning check.
terms.hear: Start with deterministic assertions.

sections.name: Receipts and revisions
sections.intro: These terms cover what a proof leaves behind and how to tell whether that evidence still applies to the code in front of you.

terms.definition: The record snack writes every time a proof runs. It contains the verdict, the revision of the code that was checked, each check with its expected and actual values, the next steps, any page errors, and a screenshot path. snack prints it, saves it to .lab-runs/snack/receipt.json, and appends a copy to .lab-runs/snack/receipts/, so earlier failures stay in the history. A receipt is a record of an evaluation. It does not mean the work passed.
terms.whyItMatters:
Your agent reads the receipt and acts on it. You ask for it instead of taking “done” on faith. To read one, work through four steps:
1. Bind: which revision was checked, and when?
2. Observe: what did the app actually do?
3. Decide: which checks failed, and what does next say?
4. Append: the new evidence joins the history.
terms.hear: Now they can show you the receipt.

terms.definition: The verdict is the receipt’s bottom line: PASS, FAIL, or ERROR. snack also reports the outcome as an exit code. 0 means PASS. 1 means FAIL, so fix the app. 2 means can’t tell, so fix the setup.
terms.whyItMatters: An agent or a CI gate can act on an exit code without reading prose. The codes also keep “fix the app” separate from “fix the setup.”
terms.hear: 0 PASS · 1 FAIL · 2 can’t tell

terms.definition: The result when the run couldn’t produce trustworthy evidence. For example, the setup is broken, the proof itself threw an error, or the judge’s API key or request failed. It exits with code 2. It is not a product failure, it never becomes a pass, and it is never a reason to change the app.
terms.whyItMatters: Treating missing evidence as a pass is how broken work slips through. A can’t-tell result tells you to fix the setup and run the check again.
terms.hear: Missing evidence never becomes a pass.

terms.definition: A fingerprint (hash) of the exact HTML that snack served when the proof ran. Each receipt belongs to one revision only. The revision is local provenance. It is not a Git commit, and it doesn’t stop an agent with shell access from changing things.
terms.whyItMatters: Lets you confirm that a PASS applies to the code in front of you. After a fix, a PASS needs fresh evidence for the new revision, and the earlier FAIL stays in the history.
terms.hear: The proof belongs to that code only.

terms.definition: A receipt that says PASS for a revision that no longer exists because the code changed after the proof ran. In the final boss exercise, a one-character edit to index.html makes snack doctor report STALE for both the build and the proof.
terms.whyItMatters: Keeps you from shipping on yesterday’s green result. After any edit, prove it again.
terms.hear: But it passed yesterday.

terms.definition: A receipt field that lists anything that threw an error in the page during the run, even when no check failed. The console-error bug shows up here and in snack console. A proof that only checks persistence still reports PASS for that bug.
terms.whyItMatters: Reading every field of the receipt, not just the verdict, catches problems your checks don’t cover yet. A “no page errors” check is the first stretch check to add.
terms.hear: It was in the receipt all along.

sections.name: Handing it to your agent
sections.intro: These terms cover the map, skill, judge, and stop rules. Together they let an agent reproduce, fix, and prove a bug by itself, and they tell it when to hand off to a human.

terms.definition: A short Markdown file, one per feature, that tells an agent where to look and what to distrust. lab/verify/features/waitlist.md answers the same questions every map answers: what sub-features exist, how a user reaches the feature, how to drive it with snack, what done means, and what the gotchas are. The idea comes from Lauren Tan’s pstack.
terms.whyItMatters: The CLI tells an agent how to look, and the map tells it where to look. Writing one map row for your own app is the first step of the take-home plan.
terms.hear: Write the map, not the manual.

terms.definition: A line in the feature map that names something which usually lies: it looks done but might not be. The waitlist’s first gotcha is that the success message appears whether or not anything was saved. Good gotchas describe behavior that a user would see and that snack can observe.
terms.whyItMatters: Each miss you discover becomes a gotcha, so the next agent knows what to double-check.
terms.hear: The success message appears whether or not anything was saved.

terms.definition: A file that teaches an agent how to use the verification tools and when to stop. lab/verify/SKILL.md lists seven steps: run doctor, read the map, reproduce, fix, prove, read the screenshot, and report. With the skill in place, the prompt can stay short: “Repro it. Fix it. Show me proof.”
terms.whyItMatters: The skill states the rule and the CLI supplies the evidence. You don’t have to repeat “remember to reload” in every prompt.
terms.hear: Repro it. Fix it. Show me proof.

terms.definition: A check for claims that a simple assertion can’t settle, such as whether a message is honest. After the agent’s fix, prove says PASS, but the screenshot reads “You’re in! Your seat is confirmed.” That breaks the waitlist-only promise. A meaning check asks one narrow yes/no question, either of a judge model or of a human reading the screenshot.
terms.whyItMatters: Shows you where persistence checks stop, and why someone still has to read what the page says.
terms.hear: It persists. It also lies.

terms.definition: A small, fast model asked one narrow question about the app’s output. pnpm snack judge runs a fresh visitor through join and reload. It then asks Jev, a model from TypeSafe, two yes/no questions. Does the message say waitlist only? Does it promise an email only if a place opens? This is the only snack command that calls a model and needs an API key.
terms.whyItMatters: Lets you check meaning automatically when exact text comparison won’t work. If your product has exactly one approved message, skip the model and compare the text.
terms.hear: Ask a fast judge one narrow question.

terms.definition: The probability of “yes” that the judge returns for each question. Jev calls this score Noul. snack applies three rules. If both scores are at least 0.9, the result is PASS. If either score is at most 0.2, the result is FAIL. Anything in between is ASK A HUMAN. A missing key or a failed request is can’t tell, never a score.
terms.whyItMatters: A probability is a signal, not proof. A score of 0.55 doesn’t mean the work is 55% done. It means the judge is torn and a human should look.
terms.hear: honest 0.01 · next step 0.02 → FAIL

terms.definition:
The rules in the skill that tell the agent when its work is finished or must be handed off:
- PASS on the current revision, with the screenshot read and the copy honest: stop and show the receipt.
- The same check still fails after two fixes: hand a human the receipt and what was tried.
- doctor shows red, or prove exits 2: fix the setup, never the app.
- The judge says ASK A HUMAN: a human reads the screenshot.
terms.whyItMatters: “Done” comes from the evidence, not from the agent’s confidence. These rules keep an agent from looping forever or declaring victory too early.
terms.hear: When to stop.

terms.definition: The number of fix attempts an agent gets on the same failing check before a human is pulled in. The workshop uses two.
terms.whyItMatters: Choose a budget and a person to escalate to for your own project. A stuck agent then hands over a receipt instead of guessing indefinitely.
terms.hear: The same failure after two fixes goes to a human.

sections.name: Testing the tester
sections.intro: These terms are about checking the checker: finding what your proof misses, turning misses into test cases, and improving the verification loop over time.

terms.definition: A secret bug that snack adds when the page loads, for the Break it quietly game. You start it with pnpm snack up --bug random. snack plays the saboteur, and you play the detective using snack commands only. The bug is one of none, memory-only, wrong-email, lost-confirmation, overpromise, or console-error. A persistence-only proof catches memory-only, wrong-email, and lost-confirmation. It still reports PASS for overpromise and console-error.
terms.whyItMatters: Tests your lever in both directions. Does it find a bug that is there, and does it stay quiet when nothing is wrong? Sometimes “it works” is the right answer.
terms.hear: Sometimes there is no bug.

terms.definition: Accepting work as done when it is actually broken. In the game this is the worst outcome. Saying “it works” when it didn’t costs 3 points, while blaming a bug that wasn’t there costs 1. When you compare versions of a verifier, false accepts are one of the first things to measure.
terms.whyItMatters: Reminds you that a verifier’s main job is to keep broken work from getting through. Confidence without evidence earns nothing.
terms.hear: Score the detective. Not the confidence.

terms.definition: A saved example of a past failure. You keep it so you can confirm the failure is still caught after later changes. Every bug your proof missed in the game becomes a new line, either a gotcha in the map or a new check in the proof.
terms.whyItMatters: Turning misses into regression cases is how the lever improves over time instead of failing the same way twice.
terms.hear: Every miss is a new line in the map.

terms.definition: A curated collection of real tasks and failure modes. The desired outcome for each case is labeled independently of what the worker claimed. Keep failures, escalations, and successes, because keeping only successes hides failure modes. Over time, saved receipts can become this dataset.
terms.whyItMatters: Lets you measure whether a change to a prompt, tool, model, or policy actually helps, instead of trusting one lucky run.
terms.hear: Receipts: evidence now, a dataset over time.

terms.definition: Cases you leave untouched while you tune. You use them to confirm a chosen change before you promote it. If you keep tuning against the same holdout cases, they effectively become training data, so set aside fresh cases for later checks.
terms.whyItMatters: Keeps your evaluation honest. A change that looks good only on cases you tuned against may not really be better.

terms.definition: Improving a system in small, measured steps. You change one thing at a time, such as a prompt, a tool, a model, or a policy. You then rerun a frozen set of cases, compare the results with a baseline, and keep the change only if the evidence supports it. In the lab, you add a “no page errors” check and keep it only if the correct app still passes and the console-error bug now fails.
terms.whyItMatters: Gives you a safe way to improve verifiers and agents. Logging is the prerequisite for this, not the improvement itself.
terms.hear: Logging is the prerequisite, not the improvement algorithm.

terms.definition: An independent check that must pass on fresh evidence before work is accepted, merged, or promoted, whatever the worker reports. snack’s exit codes let a CI gate use the proof, but the gate should still reject a missing receipt. The hosts’ own tools follow this rule: only a verifier’s receipt for the exact revision closes the work.
terms.whyItMatters: Moves the acceptance decision outside the agent’s control, so an agent can’t simply declare its own work done.
terms.hear: Neither trusts the agent’s word.

terms.definition: The parts of the browser that can answer a specific UI question. If a button fails, use the console and the sequence of actions. If data never appears, use the network requests and responses. If an interaction stalls, use performance traces and flamecharts. Chrome DevTools MCP makes these instruments available to agents.
terms.whyItMatters: Tells you which instrument to give an agent for each kind of UI symptom, and what evidence to keep. A flamechart is evidence to investigate. It does not prove that a proposed cause is correct.

quiz.question: A worker report says: form renders ✓, submit works ✓, success message ✓, Done. What’s the biggest gap in that report?
choices: It doesn’t say which model wrote the code.
None of those checks shows that the signup survives a reload. It’s a claim with no evidence of the side effect.
It should include more checkmarks for styling.
Success messages can’t be checked automatically, so the report is as good as it gets.
quiz.explanation: Every item describes what the screen showed at that moment. Reloading reveals that the record was never saved. A submit check doesn’t establish persistence, so this “done” is self-reported.

quiz.question: Why does the workshop prefer a pnpm snack prove command over a paragraph in AGENTS.md that says “always verify in a browser and reload”?
choices: Most agents ignore AGENTS.md files.
A paragraph takes up more disk space than a script.
Agents can’t run browsers, so instructions about browsers are pointless.
The command runs the same steps every time and leaves a receipt. The paragraph is re-interpreted on every run and leaves no evidence.
quiz.explanation: A lever is repeatable, can be tested, uses fewer tokens than a throwaway script, and leaves a receipt. Written instructions depend on how the agent interprets them each time.

quiz.question: pnpm snack prove exits with code 2. What should the agent do next?
choices: Fix the setup, starting with snack doctor, and leave the app alone.
Treat it as a pass, since no check failed.
Edit the app until the proof succeeds.
Loosen the proof’s expectations until it exits 0.
quiz.explanation: Exit code 2 means can’t tell: the run couldn’t produce trustworthy evidence. It isn’t a product failure, it never becomes a pass, and it’s never a reason to change the app.

quiz.question: After the reload in prove(), why should you record results with check() instead of expect()?
choices: check() is faster because it skips the browser.
expect() can’t compare strings.
expect() throws on a mismatch, and a proof that throws is reported as can’t tell instead of recording that the app is broken.
check() fixes the app automatically when a value is wrong.
quiz.explanation: check() never throws, so a missing record is written down as a failed check, and its hint becomes the next line in the receipt. A proof that throws produces can’t tell, which hides the real failure.

quiz.question: Yesterday’s receipt says PASS. This morning you added a space to the <title> in index.html, and snack doctor now reports STALE. What does that tell you?
choices: The browser cache needs clearing, and the PASS still holds.
The receipt is for a revision that no longer exists, so you need to prove it again.
A space can’t change behavior, so you can relabel the old receipt for the new revision.
Only the judge needs to be rerun. The prove result is still valid.
quiz.explanation: Every receipt belongs to one revision. When the code changes, the old proof proves nothing about the new code. Yesterday’s green result is not today’s.

quiz.question: After the agent’s fix, prove says PASS, but the screenshot reads “You’re in! Your seat is confirmed.” What’s the right conclusion?
choices: Ship it, because PASS is the final word.
The proof is wrong and should be deleted.
Add a sleep before the screenshot so it shows the right message.
prove checked persistence, not honesty. The copy needs a meaning check from a judge model or a human reading the screenshot.
quiz.explanation: The record survives the reload, so the assertions pass. Whether a message keeps the waitlist-only promise is a question about meaning, and a deterministic assertion can’t answer it.

quiz.question: Jev returns 0.55 for “Does this message say waitlist only?” How should you read that score?
choices: The feature is 55% done.
It’s a pass, because it’s above 0.5.
The judge is torn. The score falls between the thresholds, so a human should read the screenshot against the contract.
It means can’t tell, so the setup is broken.
quiz.explanation: Scores of 0.9 or higher pass, and scores of 0.2 or lower fail. Anything in between means ASK A HUMAN. The score is the probability of “yes,” which is a signal and not proof.

quiz.question: The agent has tried two fixes and the same check still fails. What does the skill say happens next?
choices: The agent stops and hands a human the receipt and what it tried.
The agent keeps trying until the check passes.
The agent switches to a weaker proof that passes.
The agent reports done, since it made real changes.
quiz.explanation: The repair budget is two fixes. After that, the agent escalates with evidence instead of guessing indefinitely.

quiz.question: In Break it quietly, which hidden bug would a proof that only checks persistence after a reload still mark as PASS?
choices: memory-only
console-error
wrong-email
lost-confirmation
quiz.explanation: memory-only, wrong-email, and lost-confirmation all change what survives a reload, so a persistence check catches them. console-error leaves persistence intact. It shows up in snack console and in the receipt’s pageErrors field. overpromise also gets past a persistence-only proof.

quiz.question: You add a “no page errors” check to your proof. When should you keep the change?
choices: Always, because more checks are always better.
Whenever the new check fails at least one app.
Only if every bug, including overpromise, now fails.
Only if the correct app still passes and the console-error bug now fails.
quiz.explanation: Hillclimbing means changing one thing and keeping it only when the evidence supports it. The correct app must still pass, and the bug the proof missed must now be caught. No assertion catches overpromise, which is why the meaning check exists.

quiz.question: In the game, saying “it works” when it didn’t costs 3 points, while blaming a bug that wasn’t there costs 1. What idea does that scoring reflect?
choices: Accepting broken work is the costliest mistake a verifier can make.
Detectives should always guess that there’s a bug.
Naming a bug without evidence earns full points.
Confidence counts for more than evidence.
quiz.explanation: A false accept lets broken work ship, while a false alarm only costs time. Naming the right bug without evidence scores 0: the game scores the detective, not their confidence.

quiz.question: Why should you leave holdout cases untouched while you tune a prompt or verifier?
choices: They are too expensive to run more than once.
Holdout cases only matter for fine-tuning.
If you tune against them repeatedly, they become training data and no longer show whether the change is really better.
They contain only successful runs.
quiz.explanation: Untouched cases give you an honest check on a chosen change. Repeated tuning against the same holdout turns it into training data, so set aside fresh cases for later checks.

quiz.question: A proof writes a signup directly into localStorage and then checks that the signup is there. Why does this proof fail the proof bar?
choices: A proof can’t read localStorage.
It takes an internal shortcut instead of the user’s path, so the real form could be broken while the proof passes.
It runs too fast for Playwright to keep up.
Writing to storage is a side effect, and proofs aren’t allowed to check side effects.
quiz.explanation: The proof bar requires the user’s path: the form, the button, and a reload. Checking side effects is required too, but the side effect has to come from the real user flow.

quiz.question: The CLI tells an agent how to look. What does the feature map add?
choices: The JSON format for snack’s output.
A full manual covering every line of the app’s code.
Where to look and what to distrust, including gotchas that usually lie.
The API key for the judge model.
quiz.explanation: The feature map covers what exists, how a user reaches it, how to drive it, what done means, and what usually lies. It is a map, not a manual.
